title: The word invites the foolish to wisdom
source_text: Ὁμολογοῦμεν δὲ πάντας ἐθέλειν παιδεῦσαι τῷ τοῦ θεοῦ, κἂν μὴ βούληται Κέλσος, λόγῳ, ὥστε καὶ μειρακίοις μεταδιδόναι τῆς ἁρμοζούσης αὐτοῖς προτροπῆς καὶ οἰκότριψιν ὑποδεικνύναι. πῶς ἐλεύθερον ἀναλαβόντες φρόνημα ἐξευγενισθεῖεν ὑπὸ τοῦ λόγου. οἱ δὲ παρ᾿ ἡμῖν πρεσβεύοντες τὸν χριστιανισμὸν ἱκανῶς φασιν ὀφειλέται εἶναι „Ἕλλησι καὶ βαρβάροις, σοφοῖς καὶ ἀνοήτοις“· οὐ γὰρ ἀρνοῦνται τὸ καὶ ἀνοήτων δεῖν τὰς ψυχὰς θεραπεύειν, ἵν᾿ ὅση δύναμις ἀποτιθέμενοι τὴν ἄγνοιαν ἐπὶ τὸ συνετώτερον σπεύδωσιν. ἀκούοντες καὶ Σολομῶντος λέγοντος· „οἱ δὲ ἄφρονες ἔνθεσθε καρδίαν“ καί· „ὅς ἐστιν ὑμῶν ἀφρονέστατος, ἐκκλινάτω πρός με, ἐνδεέσι δὲ φρενῶν παρακελεύομαι λέγουσα ἡ σοφία·“ „ἔλθετε. φάγετε τὸν ἐμὸν ἄρτον καὶ πίετε οἶνον. ὃν, ἐκέρασα ὑμῖν· ἀπολείπετε ἀφροσύνην, ἵνα ζήσητε, καὶ κατορθώσατε ἐν γνώσει σύνεσιν.“ εἴποιμ(??)δ᾿ ἂν καὶ ταῦτα διὰ τὰ ἐγκείμενα πρὸς τὸν Κέλσου λόγον· ἆρα οἱ φιλοσοφοῦντες οὐ προκαλοῦνται μειράκια ἐπὶ τὴν ἀκρόασιν; καὶ τοὺς ἀπὸ κακίστου βίου νέους οὐ παρακαλοῦσιν ἐπὶ τὰ βελτίονα; τί δὲ τοὺς οἰκότριβας οὐ βούλονται φιλοσοφεῖν; ἢ καὶ ἡμεῖς μέλλομεν ἐγκαλεῖν φιλοσόφοις οἰκότριβας ἐπ᾿ ἀρετὴν προτρεψαμένοις, Πυθαγόρᾳ μὲν τὸν Ζάμολξιν Ζήνωνι δὲ τὸν Περσαῖον καὶ χθὲς καὶ πρώην τοῖς προτρεψαμένοις Ἐπίκτητον ἐπὶ τὸ φιλοσοφεῖν; ἢ ὑμῖν μὲν, ὦ Ἕλληνες, ἔξεστι μειράκια καὶ οἰκότριβας καὶ ἀνοήτους ἀνθρώπους ἐπὶ φιλοσοφίαν καλεῖν· ἡμεῖς δὲ τοῦτο ποιοῦντες οὐ φιλανθρώπως αὐτὸ πράττομεν, τῇ ἀπὸ τοῦ λόγου ἰατρικῇ πᾶσαν λογικὴν φύσιν θεραπεῦσαι βουλόμενοι καὶ οἰκειῶσαι τῷ δημιουργήσαντι πάντα θεῷ; ἤρκει μὲν οὖν καὶ ταῦτα πρὸς τὰς Κέλσου λοιδορίας μᾶλλον ἢ κατηγορίας.
pass_a_gloss: And we agree (ὁμολογοῦμεν) that we wish to educate (παιδεῦσαι) all with the word of God, even if Celsus does not wish it, so as to share (μεταδιδόναι) also with youths the exhortation (προτροπῆς) fitting (ἁρμοζούσης) them, and to show (ὑποδεικνύναι) house-born slaves (οἰκότριψιν) how, taking up (ἀναλαβόντες) a free mind, they might be ennobled by the word. And those among us championing (πρεσβεύοντες) Christianity (χριστιανισμόν) say sufficiently (ἱκανῶς) that they are debtors (ὀφειλέται) 'to Greeks and barbarians, wise and senseless (ἀνοήτοις)'; for they do not deny (ἀρνοῦνται) that it is necessary to heal (θεραπεύειν) also the souls of the senseless, so that as far as possible putting off (ἀποτιθέμενοι) ignorance (ἄγνοιαν) they may hasten (σπεύδωσιν) toward the more intelligent (συνετώτερον); hearing also Solomon saying: 'and you senseless (ἄφρονες), put in heart', and: 'whoever of you is most senseless (ἀφρονέστατος), let him turn aside (ἐκκλινάτω) to me; and to those lacking wits I command (παρακελεύομαι), saying (λέγουσα, fem.), [I] Wisdom (ἡ σοφία): come, eat my bread (ἄρτον) and drink wine which I mixed (ἐκέρασα) for you; leave (ἀπολείπετε) folly (ἀφροσύνην), so that you may live, and set right (κατορθώσατε) understanding (σύνεσιν) in knowledge (γνώσει)'. And I would say these things also on account of the things laid against (ἐγκείμενα) in Celsus's argument: do not those philosophizing invite (προκαλοῦνται) youths to the hearing (ἀκρόασιν)? And do they not summon (παρακαλοῦσιν) the young (νέους) from a most evil life (κακίστου βίου) to better things? And what, do they not wish house-born slaves to philosophize (φιλοσοφεῖν)? Or shall we too accuse (ἐγκαλεῖν) philosophers for having turned house-born slaves to virtue, Pythagoras Zamolxis, Zeno Persaeus, and yesterday and the day before those who turned Epictetus to philosophizing? Or is it permitted (ἔξεστι) to you, O Greeks, to call youths and house-born slaves and senseless people to philosophy, but we, doing this, do not do it humanely (φιλανθρώπως), wishing to heal every rational nature with the medicine (ἰατρικῇ) from the word, and to make [it] akin (οἰκειῶσαι) to God who fashioned all things? These things then would suffice (ἤρκει) toward Celsus's revilings (λοιδορίας) rather than accusations (κατηγορίας).
pass_b_english: We admit that we want to educate everyone with the word of God, even if Celsus does not wish it, so as to give adolescents too the encouragement that suits them, and to show house-slaves how, by taking on a free spirit, they may be made noble by the word. Those among us who champion Christianity say plainly enough that they are debtors “to Greeks and barbarians, to the wise and the foolish” (Romans 1:14). For they do not deny that they must heal the souls of the foolish too, so that, as far as possible, they may lay aside their ignorance and hasten toward greater understanding. They hear Solomon also when he says, “And you who are foolish, apply your heart” (Proverbs 8:5), and, “Whoever of you is most foolish, let him turn aside to me; and to those who lack sense I, Wisdom, give this charge, saying: Come, eat my bread, and drink the wine I have mixed for you; forsake folly, that you may live, and set your understanding straight in knowledge” (Proverbs 9:4–6).

I would also say this, in view of the charges in Celsus’s argument: Do not those who practise philosophy invite adolescents to hear them? Do they not call young men who have lived the worst of lives to better things? And do they not want house-slaves to practise philosophy? Or are we too to accuse philosophers of turning house-slaves toward virtue: Pythagoras, who turned Zamolxis; Zeno, who turned Persaeus; and, only the other day, those who turned Epictetus toward philosophy? Or is it allowed to you Greeks to call adolescents, house-slaves and foolish people to philosophy, while we, when we do this, do not do it out of love for humanity, though we wish to heal every rational nature with the medicine of the word and to bring it into kinship with God, who made all things?
This, then, would be enough in answer to Celsus’s abuse, for it is abuse rather than accusation.

choices.choice: Proverbs 8:5 LXX reads 'and you who are uninstructed (ἀπαίδευτοι), apply your heart'; Origen's text has ἄφρονες ('foolish'). Proverbs 9:4-6 is quoted with variants from the LXX (ἀφρονέστατος 'most foolish' for ἄφρων; παρακελεύομαι λέγουσα ἡ σοφία 'I, Wisdom, give this charge, saying' for εἶπεν 'she said'; 'my bread' singular for 'my loaves'; where Origen has 'that you may live', the LXX of 9:6 has 'that you may reign for ever, and seek prudence', while the Hebrew has 'and live'); translated as Origen gives it. λέγουσα ἡ σοφία stands inside Koetschau's quotation marks, with Wisdom as the speaker of the whole verse, so the English keeps it inside the quotation as 'I, Wisdom, ... saying'. Chapter numbering of Proverbs 8-9 is the same in LXX and English. πρεσβεύοντες rendered 'champion' (LSJ: hold in honour, put first); 'serve as ambassadors of' is also possible and may echo 2 Corinthians 5:20, but this is uncertain and left uncited. The staged text has 'εἴποιμ(??)δ᾿ ἂν', a scan defect for εἴποιμι δ᾿ ἄν ('I would say'). τὰ ἐγκείμενα ('the things pressed/laid') read as Celsus's charges; it could also mean 'the points that bear on Celsus's argument'. τοὺς ἀπὸ κακίστου βίου νέους is read as 'young men who come from the worst life', i.e. who have lived it. Zamolxis as Pythagoras's slave is reported by Herodotus (Histories 4.95); Persaeus as Zeno's household slave by Diogenes Laertius (Lives 7.36); Epictetus, once a slave, was taught by Musonius Rufus. These are historical allusions, not quotations, so no inline source is given. 'Only the other day' renders χθὲς καὶ πρώην (literally 'yesterday and the day before').

Proverbs 9:4: 'I give this charge,' says Wisdom' -> 'I, Wisdom, give this charge, saying:'; the Greek λέγουσα ('saying', fem.) was dropped and ἡ σοφία is the subject inside the quotation, not an outside frame.
Corrected the Proverbs 9:6 note: the LXX has 'that you may reign for ever' in place of (not before) 'that you may live'; Origen's reading matches the Hebrew.
τοὺς ἀπὸ κακίστου βίου νέους: 'urge young men away from the worst way of life' -> 'call young men who have lived the worst of lives to better things'.
Removed archaic 'What,' (τί δέ) and added 'too' for καὶ ἡμεῖς ('are we too to accuse').
Checked Romans 1:14, Proverbs 8:5 and 9:4-6 against the verses; Herodotus 4.95 and Diogenes Laertius 7.36 left in notes only.
